drills.title: A class with a constructor and toString
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines into a Product class: private fields, a constructor that fills them, a toString and a main that prints one product. The constructor and toString can go in either order. Two lines do not belong.
drills.explain: A constructor has the class name and no return type (void Product(...) would be an ordinary method, and new Product(...) would not find a constructor). Inside it the parameter hides the field, so this.name = name copies the parameter into the field; plain name = name only assigns the parameter to itself. toString decides how println shows the object.

drills.title: A counter shared by every account
drills.prompt: Fill the blanks so every Account keeps its own owner while all accounts share one counter of how many were opened.
drills.explain: A static field exists once for the whole class, so both new Account(...) calls increase the same counter. Without static every object would have its own opened and Account.getOpened() could not be called on the class. this.owner means the field of this object; Java has no self (that is Python). final would forbid opened++.

drills.title: Same object or same SKU?
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
code: @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Sku that && code.equals(that.code); }
drills.explain: == asks whether two variables point at the very same object. a and b are two separate objects, so it is false, while c is another name for a, so it is true. equals compares the codes, so a.equals(b) is true, and the HashSet (which uses equals and hashCode) keeps only one of them.

drills.title: The price that stays 0.0
drills.prompt: The program runs, but it prints a price of 0.0 instead of 10.0. Click the faulty line, then choose the fix.
drills.explain: Inside the constructor the parameter price hides the field price. price = price copies the parameter onto itself and never touches the field, which keeps its default 0.0. Write this.price = price. this.price = this.price also does nothing, price = this.price copies in the wrong direction, and Product.price would look for a static field.

drills.title: Review the AI's BankAccount
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote this BankAccount. It compiles and runs, but tick the real problems (there are three).
code: private final List<String> history = new ArrayList<>();

issues.why: Any code can write acc.balance = -100 and skip every rule. Make it private and expose it through a getBalance() method plus deposit and withdraw that check their input.

issues.text: getHistory returns the internal list itself
issues.why: The caller receives the same list object, so acc.getHistory().clear() wipes the account's record (main does exactly that). Return a copy: new ArrayList<>(history), or List.copyOf(history).

issues.text: deposit accepts any amount, including zero and negative numbers
issues.why: deposit(-500) would quietly take money out and log it as a deposit. The class should protect its own rule: if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(...).

non_issues.text: history is final, so add() cannot work on it
non_issues.why: final fixes which list the variable points to, not what is inside the list. Adding entries is allowed.

non_issues.text: history should be created inside the constructor
non_issues.why: A field initializer runs for every new object, so each account gets its own list. Both styles are fine.
A final field with no setter is what you want for something that must never change after construction.
Package-private is fine inside one package, and there is no rule that every method must be public. The real gap is what deposit checks, not who can call it.

drills.explain: In generated classes check three places: fields (private?), anything a getter hands out (a live list or a copy?), and every method that changes state (does it guard its own rules?).
